1.patient_information_and_chief_complain.text: The patient is a 59-year-old man who was admitted to our Department of Respiratory and Critical Care Medicine on Day 0, with the chief complaint of "cough and sputum production with hemoptysis for more than 2 months, with recurrence for more than 4 days." More than 2 months earlier, after catching a cold, the patient developed cough with white foamy sputum, accompanied by blood-streaked sputum in a small amount, and shortness of breath on exertion, without chills, fever, chest tightness, palpitations, chest pain, or other discomfort. He presented to a local hospital, where CBC showed "WBC 9.14*10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 70.1%." Chest CT suggested "multiple patchy opacities in all lobes of both lungs with indistinct margins, with air bronchograms within them." The patient was then diagnosed with "lobar pneumonia" and sequentially received anti-infective treatment with "ceftazidime," "levofloxacin," and "ceftriaxone," as well as expectorant treatment including "bromhexine." After 10 days of treatment, his symptoms improved and he was discharged. After discharge, he still had a mild cough with a small amount of white foamy sputum. Thereafter, more than 1 month before the second admission, after another cold exposure, the patient's cough worsened again, with orange-red sputum, total daily amount about 15 ml, accompanied by fever with a self-measured temperature of 38.0℃, marked dyspnea, and no chest pain. He sought care at a hospital in Lanzhou, where CBC showed "WBC 10.89*10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 69.0%." ECG suggested "atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response." Chest CT showed "scattered flocculent increased-density opacities in both lungs, most prominent in the lower lobes of both lungs; bilateral pleural effusions." Echocardiography showed "rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis with insufficiency; left atrial enlargement; elevated pulmonary artery pressure (moderate)." He sequentially received anti-infective treatment with "Tienam" and "cefoperazone-tazobactam"; during this period, he also received diagnostic anti-TB treatment with "isoniazid + rifampin," as well as cardiotonic therapy, diuresis, anticoagulation, ventricular rate control, and other treatments. The amount of hemoptysis decreased significantly, and he was discharged after his temperature normalized. Four days before admission, the patient's cough worsened again, with white sticky sputum containing a small amount of blood, accompanied by low-grade fever with a maximum temperature of 37.7 degrees, without chest pain or dyspnea. He came to our hospital emergency department for further diagnosis and treatment. CBC showed WBC 8.16 *10^9/l and neutrophil percentage 70.6%; chest CT suggested "scattered patchy opacities, linear opacities, and areas of consolidation in both lungs; increased and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes; cardiomegaly, calcification of the aortic wall, bilateral coronary artery walls, and mitral valve; right pleural thickening and calcification; small bilateral pleural effusions." During emergency hospitalization, anti-TB drugs were discontinued, and after treatment with "moxifloxacin" for infection, "rivaroxaban 10mg qd" for anticoagulation, correction of cardiac function, and other treatments, he was admitted to our department. Since the onset of illness, the patient has had fair mental status, sleep, and appetite; normal bowel and bladder function; and weight loss of about 2 kg. Past history: More than 10 years ago, the patient was found to have elevated blood glucose, with fasting blood glucose up to 8+ mmol/L, and intermittently took oral hypoglycemic agents, but did not undergo long-term blood glucose monitoring thereafter. More than 6 years ago, he was also found to have rheumatic heart disease with severe mitral stenosis, insufficiency, atrial fibrillation, and coronary atherosclerotic heart disease. He had previously been taking long-term oral warfarin for anticoagulation and atorvastatin for lipid lowering, without INR monitoring. More than 1 month earlier, INR was found to be 7.68 at a hospital in Lanzhou, and anticoagulation was changed to rivaroxaban 10mg qd. In addition, the patient has been known to be a hepatitis B virus carrier since childhood and has not received antiviral treatment. He denies a history of TB, chronic bronchitis, hypertension, and other diseases. He has lived long-term in Lanzhou, Gansu Province. He has no history of food or drug allergies, and no history of surgery or trauma. He smoked for more than 20 years and quit more than 10 years ago. He drinks small amounts of alcohol occasionally. Family history is unremarkable. Physical examination on admission: T: 36.7℃, P: 132/min, R: 22/min, BP: 129/80 mmHg. He was alert, in fair general condition, with a chronic ill appearance. No jaundice of the skin or sclera. No enlargement of superficial lymph nodes was palpable throughout the body. Jugular veins were normal. Cardiac dullness was enlarged to the left. Irregular heart rhythm. A diastolic rumbling murmur was audible in the mitral valve auscultation area. No abnormalities of the thorax were seen. Percussion of both lungs was resonant. Scattered moist rales were audible in both lungs, without pleural friction rub. The abdomen was flat and soft, with no tenderness or rebound tenderness throughout, and no abdominal masses were palpable. Liver and spleen were not palpable below the costal margins. No edema of either lower extremity. Ancillary examinations (at local hospital on Day -53): WBC 10.89*10^9/L, neutrophil percentage 69.0%, blood glucose 15.15mmol/l, PT 81.1 seconds, INR 7.68, PCT 0.046 ng/ml, CRP 145.99 mg/l, respiratory pathogen panel of nine items negative. Chest CT: pneumonia in both lungs, bilateral pleural effusions, aortic and coronary atherosclerosis, enlarged cardiac silhouette, small pericardial effusion, calcified mediastinal lymph nodes. Echocardiography: rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis with mild-to-moderate insufficiency, mild aortic regurgitation, mild mitral regurgitation. Ancillary examinations (West China emergency department): CBC showed WBC 8.16 *10^9/l and neutrophil percentage 70.6%. Urinalysis, stool routine, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were normal. Arterial blood gas analysis: PH 7.484, PO2 74.6mmHg, PCO2 31.8mmHg, Lac 1.1mmol/L, HCO3- 23.4mmol/L. Coagulation studies showed: prothrombin time 12.9 seconds, international normalized ratio 1.18, activated partial thromboplastin time 34.9 seconds, D-dimer 0.93 mg/l FEU. Hemoglobin A1c 8.0%. Urinary sodium peptide 460pg/ml, myocardial markers normal. PCT less than 0.02ng/ml, ESR 47.0mm/h. Bedside ECG showed: atrial flutter (2:1 conduction). Echocardiography showed: severe mitral stenosis with mild regurgitation, mild tricuspid regurgitation, moderate pulmonary hypertension, mildly reduced left ventricular systolic function (LV 48, LA 60, RV 21, EF 49%). Chest CT (Day -2) showed: 1. Scattered patchy opacities, linear opacities, and areas of consolidation in both lungs. 2. Increased and enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes. 3. Cardiomegaly, mainly left atrial enlargement, calcification of the aortic wall, bilateral coronary artery walls, and mitral valve. 4. Right pleural thickening and calcification, small bilateral pleural effusions.

differential_diagnoses.name: Infectious pneumonia (community-acquired pneumonia/bronchopneumonia, possibly recurrent or incompletely resolved)
supporting_evidence: Chief complaint: 'Cough and sputum production with hemoptysis for more than 2 months, recurrent episode for more than 4 days'; during the course of illness, symptoms worsened after catching a cold, with sputum production, low-grade fever or fever.
More than 2 months ago, chest CT showed "multiple patchy opacities in all lobes of both lungs, with indistinct margins and air bronchograms within them"
More than 1 month ago, chest CT showed scattered patchy increased-density opacities in both lungs, more prominent in the bilateral lower lobes; bilateral pleural effusion

This chest CT showed “scattered patchy opacities, linear opacities, and consolidative opacities in both lungs”; the accompanying images show multiple patchy/consolidative opacities in both lungs, more prominent in the bilateral lower lungs.
On physical examination, scattered moist rales were audible in both lungs.
Symptoms had previously improved and the patient was discharged after anti-infective treatment, suggesting that the lesion was to some extent related to the infectious process.
CRP 145.99 mg/l elevated, ESR 47.0 mm/h
opposing_evidence: On multiple occasions, the white blood cell count was only mildly elevated or close to normal; this time the white blood cell count was 8.16*10^9/L, with a neutrophil percentage of 70.6%
PCT 0.046 ng/ml and the current PCT <0.02 ng/ml do not support severe bacterial infection.

The lesion has been recurrent and prolonged for more than 2 months, and has continued to recur despite treatment with multiple antibacterial agents, which is not consistent with the typical course of simple common bacterial pneumonia.
There is significant underlying heart disease and anticoagulant use, suggesting that the hemoptysis and imaging changes may not be fully explained by infection.

differential_diagnoses.name: Cardiogenic pulmonary congestion/pulmonary edema with hemoptysis (caused by rheumatic heart disease and severe mitral stenosis)
supporting_evidence: History of confirmed rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis with regurgitation, atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter, left atrial enlargement, elevated pulmonary artery pressure
This echocardiogram showed severe mitral stenosis, mildly reduced measured left ventricular systolic function, and moderate pulmonary hypertension.

Chest CT showed “cardiomegaly, predominantly left atrial enlargement,” with “small bilateral pleural effusions”; the accompanying images show an enlarged cardiac silhouette and bilateral pleural effusions.
Symptoms include obvious shortness of breath, chest tightness, and dyspnea on exertion, consistent with cardiogenic pulmonary congestion/pulmonary edema.
Blood-streaked sputum or expectoration of orange-red sputum may be seen in pulmonary venous hypertension caused by mitral stenosis
After treatment at an outside hospital with cardiotonic therapy, diuresis, and ventricular rate control, the patient's hemoptysis volume decreased significantly.
opposing_evidence: In addition to pleural effusion, imaging also shows scattered patchy opacities, areas of consolidation, and air bronchograms in both lungs, which is more suggestive of concomitant pulmonary parenchymal disease rather than simple cardiogenic edema.
During the course of the disease, recurrent fever, markedly elevated CRP, and moist crackles were noted, suggesting possible concurrent infection or other inflammatory lesions.
The bilateral lung lesions are not distributed in a typical symmetric central bat-wing pattern.

differential_diagnoses.name: Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage syndrome/pulmonary hemorrhage (anticoagulation-related or related to pulmonary venous hypertension)
supporting_evidence: Persistent hemoptysis or blood-streaked sputum; previously coughed up "orange-red sputum"

Previously on long-term warfarin anticoagulation without INR monitoring; more than 1 month ago, INR was 7.68, indicating a previous significant bleeding risk due to overanticoagulation; later switched to rivaroxaban
Severe mitral stenosis can cause elevated pulmonary venous pressure and can also cause alveolar hemorrhage and hemoptysis
Chest CT and the accompanying images show multiple patchy opacities/consolidative opacities in both lungs, which may be seen in alveolar hemorrhage.
Arterial blood gas showed mild hypoxemia (PO2 74.6 mmHg)
opposing_evidence: In the first phase, no information indicating anemia was found, and there was no indication of a progressive decrease in hemoglobin.
During the clinical course, fever, elevated CRP, and moist rales were also present, suggesting that hemorrhage alone cannot fully explain all manifestations.
This coagulation panel showed PT 12.9 seconds and INR 1.18; there is currently no clear laboratory evidence indicating that the patient remains in an overanticoagulated state.

differential_diagnoses.name: pulmonary tuberculosis
supporting_evidence: Cough, hemoptysis, low-grade fever/fever, weight loss of approximately 2 kg, consistent with common clinical clues of TB

Chest CT showed an increased number and enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes; previously there were also “mediastinal lymph node calcification” and “right pleural thickening and calcification,” suggesting the possibility of prior pleural/mediastinal granulomatous disease.
Recurrent, persistent multifocal lesions in both lungs, with repeated episodes despite standard anti-infective therapy
At an outside hospital, diagnostic anti-TB treatment with "isoniazid + rifampin" had been administered, indicating that TB had once been strongly suspected clinically.
opposing_evidence: Stage 1: confirm the history of "denies TB"

Imaging findings are mainly scattered patchy opacities and areas of consolidation in both lungs, more pronounced in the bilateral lower lungs, and pleural effusion, rather than the typical upper lobe cavitary tuberculosis pattern.
Negative nine-respiratory-pathogen testing does not support TB; in the first stage, no positive evidence from sputum smear, TB-DNA, or TB immunologic testing was provided either

After anti-infective therapy and cardiac function treatment at an outside hospital, body temperature returned to normal and hemoptysis decreased, suggesting that the condition may not be primarily driven by active TB.

differential_diagnoses.name: Organizing pneumonia (cryptogenic or secondary)
supporting_evidence: The clinical course is subacute, prolonged, and recurrent, with cough, shortness of breath, and low-grade fever; only partial relief after antibacterial therapy, followed by recurrence.

Repeated chest CT scans showed multiple patchy opacities, linear opacities, and areas of consolidation in both lungs; the accompanying images show multifocal consolidation/patchy opacities predominantly in the peripheral and lower lungs bilaterally, consistent with one of the common imaging patterns of organizing pneumonia
Inflammatory markers may be elevated, but PCT remains persistently low, which does not support typical severe bacterial infection
The lesions in both lungs are not confined to a single fixed lobe and are multifocally distributed.
opposing_evidence: There is definite severe mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation, pleural effusion, and cardiomegaly; cardiogenic factors may explain some of the imaging findings and symptoms.
Hemoptysis is present; although it can be seen in organizing pneumonia, it is not the most common initial presentation.
In the first stage, no pathology, bronchoscopy, or specific imaging signs were provided to support this diagnosis.

differential_diagnoses.name: Pulmonary malignant tumor (such as lung adenocarcinoma, especially mucinous adenocarcinoma / lepidic growth pattern, or other pulmonary tumors)
supporting_evidence: 59-year-old man with a smoking history of more than 20 years
Recurrent cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss of approximately 2 kg are common warning symptoms of lung cancer
Chest CT showed multiple patchy opacities/consolidative opacities in both lungs with persistent nonresolving lesions, and increased number and enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes
The accompanying image shows multifocal areas of consolidation in both lungs; some tumors, especially mucinous adenocarcinoma, may present with a pneumonia-like appearance.
opposing_evidence: In the first-stage imaging, no definite space-occupying mass, lobulation with spiculation, cavitation, or obstructive changes were described.

During the course of the illness, there was fever, a marked elevation in CRP, and prior symptomatic improvement after anti-infective treatment, further suggesting an inflammatory or infectious process.
Bilateral pleural effusions, cardiomegaly, and severe mitral stenosis suggest underlying cardiopulmonary disease that better explains the symptoms

recommended_exams.exam: Immune markers (anti-streptolysin O, immunoglobulin A, immunoglobulin M, C3, C4, ANCA, GBM, T-cell subsets)

recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 59-year-old man with recurrent cough, sputum production, and hemoptysis for more than 2 months. Chest CT showed recurrent multiple patchy opacities and areas of consolidation in both lungs, and the lesions remained persistent or even progressed at one point despite multiple anti-infective treatments. It is necessary to clarify as soon as possible whether this represents infection, tumor, alveolar hemorrhage, or other noninfectious lesions. Bronchoscopy under general anesthesia allows direct visualization of the site of endobronchial bleeding, mucosal lesions, and secretions under safer and more adequate airway control, and enables specimen collection such as lavage and brushings. This examination helps exclude an endobronchial tumor and determine whether there is evidence of active airway infection or alveolar hemorrhage. At the same time, given the patient's atrial fibrillation, severe mitral stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, and history of anticoagulation, it also facilitates assessment and reduction of procedure-related risk under close monitoring.

The patient has persistent hemoptysis and atypical imaging lesions. Previous sputum culture, sputum pathogen testing, and multiple infectious screening tests were negative. There is insufficient evidence for uncomplicated bacterial pneumonia, while pulmonary tumor, TB, and alveolar hemorrhage have not been completely excluded. Fiberoptic bronchoscopy allows direct visualization of the glottis, carina, and bronchi at all levels to determine whether there is focal bleeding, luminal obstruction, mucosal hyperemia and swelling, or a neoplasm, thereby clarifying the source of hemoptysis and the nature of the lesion. In this case, this examination is an important step in distinguishing endobronchial lesions from lesions at the pulmonary parenchymal/alveolar level, and provides a basis for subsequent brush cytology, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid submission for testing, and treatment decision-making.

The patient has multifocal infiltrative opacities in both lungs with recurrent blood-tinged sputum. The response to anti-infective therapy is inconsistent with the imaging changes, and the initial screening for infection, immune-related disease, and tumor-related disease has not provided a clear direction; therefore, it is necessary to obtain deep lower respiratory tract specimens. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid is helpful for cytologic and etiologic analysis to determine whether there are malignant cells and clues to bacterial/fungal/TB-related infection, and to assess alveolar hemorrhage in conjunction with the appearance of the lavage fluid and subsequent staining. This examination directly addresses the core clinical question in this case: whether the bilateral pulmonary lesions are infection, tumor, or diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, which is critical for establishing the diagnosis and deciding whether to continue anti-infective therapy or shift to management of a noninfectious cause.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: Further bronchial brush cytology showed no malignant cells.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient is a 59-year-old man with a smoking history of more than 20 years, recurrent hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent nonresolving pulmonary consolidation, and increased number and enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes; a pulmonary neoplasm, especially pneumonic-type lung cancer, needs to be a key focus of evaluation. Bronchial brushing can obtain cytologic specimens from suspicious mucosa or lesion areas under bronchoscopy to determine whether malignant cell shedding is present. Although imaging did not show a typical solitary mass, because the lesion has persisted and recurred and anti-infective treatment has not been typically effective, brushing examination is of important value for excluding tumors related to endobronchial or proximal lesions and for guiding whether further pathologic sampling is needed.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: No malignant cells detected on sputum smear
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has chronic cough and sputum production with recurrent blood-streaked sputum. Sputum specimen testing is a fundamental, low-risk examination for obtaining exfoliated respiratory tract cells and etiologic information. Because the differential diagnosis in this case includes both lung tumor, infection, and alveolar hemorrhage, sputum smear may be performed first to screen for malignant cells or certain clues to infection, as a complement before and after invasive examinations. Especially when the patient has underlying heart disease and a history of anticoagulation/previous over-anticoagulation, initially completing the evaluation with less invasive methods may help improve diagnostic efficiency and reduce risk.

The patient has recurrent hemoptysis. Imaging shows multiple patchy opacities and consolidations in both lungs, along with high-risk background factors for alveolar hemorrhage including severe mitral stenosis, pulmonary hypertension, long-term anticoagulation, and a history of markedly elevated INR. Clinically, there is a strong need to determine whether hemosiderin-laden macrophages are present. Prussian blue staining is used to detect iron deposition within macrophages after hemorrhage and is an important adjunctive method for evaluating alveolar hemorrhage. This test is intended to provide cytologic evidence for diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, help distinguish the lesions from simple infection or tumor, and influence subsequent treatment strategy selection regarding anti-infective therapy, anticoagulation, and management of the underlying cardiac disease.

recommended_exams.exam: Prussian blue staining of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid
recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: No malignant cells were found in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, Prussian blue stain (-)
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: Compared with sputum specimens, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid better reflects the true conditions within the alveolar spaces. The patient had recurrent hemoptysis and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and the lesion changes were more closely related to the amount of bloody sputum and less correlated with the intensity of anti-infective therapy; therefore, evidence of hemorrhage needed to be sought at the alveolar level. Prussian blue staining of the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was performed mainly to determine whether hemosiderin-laden macrophages were present, thereby supporting or refuting diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. This result is of key value in distinguishing infectious pneumonia, neoplastic lesions, and alveolar hemorrhage, and also helps explain why the lesions were instead absorbed after discontinuation of anti-infective therapy.

During the course of the illness, the patient had fever, elevated CRP and ESR, crackles, and bilateral pulmonary consolidation opacities; infectious pneumonia was always an important differential consideration. However, PCT remained persistently low, the white blood cell count was not elevated, and the condition still recurred despite broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy, making the evidence for simple bacterial infection insufficient. Smear examination of bronchoscopy or lavage specimens can rapidly look for clues to pathogens such as bacteria, fungi, or mycobacteria, helping determine whether intensified anti-infective treatment still needs to be continued. The clinical purpose of this examination is to exclude infection as much as possible, as it is the most common etiology and has a completely different treatment pathway, and to avoid mistreating noninfectious alveolar hemorrhage as infection.

Because the patient's pulmonary lesions have been prolonged and recurrent, and he has previously received multiple anti-infective therapies including ceftazidime, levofloxacin, ceftriaxone, Tienam, cefoperazone-tazobactam, and moxifloxacin, if infection is still present, identifying the pathogen is extremely important for subsequent medication selection. Culture testing can perform pathogen identification and antimicrobial susceptibility testing on lower respiratory tract specimens, addressing whether there is persistent infection with common bacteria, opportunistic pathogens, or other special pathogens. In this case, the culture results are directly related to whether anti-infective therapy can be safely discontinued or adjusted, and, together with the subsequent evolution of the lesions on CT, help determine whether the lesions are mainly caused by noninfectious factors.

The patient has long-standing diffuse infiltrative opacities in both lungs that have not resolved; multiple prior courses of antibacterial treatment produced no decisive improvement, and routine pathogen testing was negative. Further exclusion of fungal infection is needed, especially diseases such as invasive aspergillosis, which can present with persistent pulmonary opacities and hemoptysis. The GM test can provide fungus-related clues in specimens such as lavage fluid, helping differentiate fungal infection from noninfectious alveolar hemorrhage, organizing pneumonia, or tumor. The significance of this test is to avoid missing diseases that require specific antifungal therapy, while also providing a basis for discontinuing empiric anti-infective treatment and shifting toward other etiologies.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: (Day +5) Repeat chest CT: after 1 week of anti-infective therapy, repeat chest CT showed worsening of the lesions
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient’s core problem is that the nature of the bilateral lung lesions is unclear and the disease course is dynamically complex. After 1 week of anti-infective treatment following admission, although the symptoms were somewhat relieved, repeat CT showed worsening of the lesions instead. This imaging evolution is critical for determining whether the lesions are driven by bacterial infection. The purpose of repeat chest CT is to objectively assess changes in the extent, density, and distribution of the lesions, and to observe whether they are consistent with the clinical symptoms and treatment response, thereby addressing the key clinical decision of whether to continue management as infection or to consider noninfectious causes. In this case, worsening on CT suggests that infection alone is insufficient to explain the findings, prompting further consideration of noninfectious etiologies such as alveolar hemorrhage.

The patient has definite rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis, atrial fibrillation/atrial flutter, left atrial enlargement, pulmonary hypertension, and bilateral pleural effusions; the symptoms also include shortness of breath and dyspnea, so cardiogenic pulmonary edema or pulmonary congestion has always been an important differential diagnosis. BNP testing is used to assess whether there is heart failure-related volume overload and cardiogenic dyspnea, and plays an important role in distinguishing cardiogenic pulmonary opacities from infection, tumor, or alveolar hemorrhage. In this case, repeatedly normal BNP levels weaken the explanation of typical heart failure pulmonary edema and help shift attention to alveolar hemorrhage and pulmonary venous hypertension-related changes caused by valvular disease.

recommended_exams.basis_in_stage3_input: During hospitalization at an outside hospital, repeat testing showed a marked elevation in INR.
recommended_exams.why_order_this_exam: The patient has been taking oral warfarin anticoagulation long-term for atrial fibrillation and had not undergone regular INR monitoring in the past. An outside hospital previously measured an INR of 7.68, indicating marked over-anticoagulation. At the same time, the patient had recurrent hemoptysis and persistent bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and the clinical team must evaluate the possibility of anticoagulation-related alveolar hemorrhage. The core purpose of INR testing is to clarify coagulation status and bleeding risk, determine whether the hemoptysis and pulmonary imaging changes are related to excessive anticoagulation, and provide a basis for whether to subsequently adjust, hold, or switch the anticoagulation regimen. In combination with the patient's severe mitral stenosis and pulmonary hypertension, the INR result is critical for confirming the cause of bleeding, balancing thrombotic and bleeding risks, and guiding treatment decisions.

7.key_confirmatory_exam_information.text: Bronchoscopy, fiberoptic bronchoscopy examination, and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid were performed under general anesthesia. Findings under bronchoscopy: no abnormalities of the glottis or carina; a small amount of purulent secretions in the bilateral bronchi at all levels; after suctioning via bronchoscopy, hyperemia and swelling of the mucosa on the anterolateral wall of the distal left main bronchus were seen; the remaining bronchial mucosa at all levels bilaterally was smooth, and the lumens were patent. Further bronchial brushing showed no malignant cells; sputum smear showed no malignant cells, Prussian blue stain (-); bronchoalveolar lavage fluid showed no malignant cells, Prussian blue stain (-); smear and culture were negative; GM test 0.51 GMI. On (Day +5), repeat chest CT was performed. After 1 week of anti-infective treatment, repeat chest CT showed progression of the lesions. In view of some relief of the patient's cough and sputum symptoms and insufficient evidence for infection or immune system disease, moxifloxacin was discontinued, and low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulation was continued. The patient had no fever, and hemoptysis gradually improved. One week later, repeat chest CT indicated that the bilateral lung lesions had been absorbed compared with before. Multiple BNP tests were normal. The patient had rheumatic heart disease, severe mitral stenosis, and moderate pulmonary hypertension, and had previously been on long-term warfarin anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation without INR monitoring. During hospitalization at an outside hospital, repeat INR was significantly elevated. The amount of hemoptysis was closely related to the pulmonary imaging findings; as the hemoptysis decreased, the pulmonary lesions were also absorbed. No typical bright red fluid was seen in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.

diagnostic_basis: Past medical history: rheumatic heart disease (mitral stenosis), long-term warfarin anticoagulation; INR was not monitored before disease onset

From the patient's symptoms, imaging findings, and the timeline of anticoagulant therapy, it can be seen that the patient's imaging findings are related to sputum production, especially blood-tinged sputum, and are not strongly correlated with the intensity of anti-infective therapy.

Especially on the three CT scans from 4-3 to 4-17, the second follow-up chest CT showed increased pulmonary lesions, whereas on this basis the lesions instead improved after discontinuation of anti-infective treatment, fully indicating that the pulmonary lesions were very likely caused by noninfectious factors.

treatment_plan: Transferred to Cardiothoracic Surgery for mitral valve replacement + tricuspid valvuloplasty
On Day -79, treatment was given with ceftazidime, levofloxacin, and ceftriaxone.

From Day -2 to Day +5, low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulation therapy was administered
From Day +5 to Day +12, moxifloxacin was discontinued, and low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulation therapy was continued
